---
title: "Day 11 — Can we trust this table?"
---

[Lecture slides](../lectures/11-data-quality/lec.qmd) · [Quiz](11-data-quality-quiz.qmd) · [Weekly revision](quiz.qmd)

## Today's question

A labmate has exported the seedling measurements from the lab spreadsheet into
`data/seedlings-messy.csv`. Before calculating anything you want to know whether
the file really holds 24 plants with sensible lengths. R will calculate a mean
from any table, so the checking is up to you. Today you inspect the export,
repair what the source records support, and save a cleaned copy while the raw
file stays unchanged.

The study itself is described in the [data dictionary](../data/README.md). The
source records for this export are in
[`data/field-notes.txt`](../data/field-notes.txt); read them before you start.

**Save today:** `day11-cleaning.R` in the project root,
`output/seedlings-cleaned.csv` and `output/cleaning-notes.txt`.

## Reading every column as text

Start `day11-cleaning.R` with:

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
raw <- read_csv("data/seedlings-messy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
                col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), trim_ws = FALSE)
dim(raw)
```

Normally `read_csv()` guesses which columns hold numbers. Here
`cols(.default = col_character())` reads every column as text, so an odd entry
stays exactly as it was typed, and `trim_ws = FALSE` keeps any spaces at the
start or end of a value. `dim()` gives 25 rows and 4 columns, although the
study has 24 plants.

## Is any plant in the file twice?

Use `count()` to find out which plant IDs appear more than once, then look at
those rows:

```{r}
raw |> count(plant_id) |> filter(n > 1)
filter(raw, plant_id == "P01")
```

`count()` counts the rows for each ID and `filter(n > 1)` keeps the repeated
ones. P01 appears twice, and its two rows are identical in every column. The
study has one row per plant, and the field notes confirm that the second row is
an accidental repeat of the import, so one of them can go. In a design with one
row per time point a repeated ID would be normal, which is why you compare
whole rows and the design before removing anything.

## Which treatment labels are used?

Use `unique()` to find out how the treatment was written:

```{r}
unique(raw$treatment)
```

There are four spellings: `"control"`, `"Control"`, `"treated"` and `"treated "`
with a space at the end. R treats them as four different groups, so a group
summary would give four rows instead of two. According to the field notes,
P03's `Control` means control and P15's trailing space is an export mistake.

## Are the lengths plausible?

Use `filter()` with `%in%` to look at the plants the field notes mention:

```{r}
filter(raw, plant_id %in% c("P06", "P18", "P21"))
```

`%in%` keeps the rows whose ID is in the listed set. P18's initial length is the
text `18.7 mm`, and the notes confirm it was measured in millimetres. P21's final
length is 4.38, much shorter than its initial 23.6 mm; the source notebook
records **43.8 mm**, so the value was typed in centimetres. P06 has no final
length, and the notes say that reading is unavailable.

A value is changed only when a source record supports the change. A small or
large value on its own is not a reason, because plants really do vary.

## Repairing a copy in code

```{r}
cleaned <- raw |>
  mutate(treatment = tolower(trimws(treatment)),
         initial_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P18", "18.7", initial_mm),
         final_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P21", "43.8", final_mm)) |>
  distinct() |>
  mutate(initial_mm = parse_double(initial_mm),
         final_mm = parse_double(final_mm),
         growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
```

Each line carries out one sentence of the field notes. `trimws()` removes the
spaces around a value and `tolower()` turns `Control` into `control`.
`if_else(condition, yes, no)` replaces a value only in the row of the named plant.
`distinct()` removes rows that are identical in every column, which here is the
second P01. `parse_double()` then turns the checked text into numbers, and P06's
empty final length becomes `NA`, R's code for a missing value. The CSV file is
never edited, so anyone can rerun the script and see every repair.

## Does the cleaned table have 24 plants?

Use `nrow()`, `anyDuplicated()` and `sum(is.na())` to find out whether the repair
left one row per plant and how many growth values are missing:

```{r}
nrow(cleaned)
anyDuplicated(cleaned$plant_id)
sum(is.na(cleaned$growth_mm))
cleaned |> count(treatment)
write_csv(cleaned, "output/seedlings-cleaned.csv")
```

You should get 24 rows, 0 (no ID is repeated), 1 missing growth value, and 12
plants in each group. So the control group has 12 plants but only 11 usable
growth values. `write_csv()` saves the cleaned table as a new file next to the
other outputs.

## Why P06 stays missing

Use `mean()` to find out the average growth of all plants:

```{r}
mean(cleaned$growth_mm)
mean(cleaned$growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The first line gives `NA`: one value is unknown, and R will not guess. With
`na.rm = TRUE` ("remove NA") R averages the 23 available values and gives
**18.49 mm**, which you report as the mean of 23 of the 24 plants.

Writing 0 for P06's final length would claim a measurement nobody made. P06
started at 24.7 mm, so it would "grow" −24.7 mm and pull the overall mean down
to 16.69 mm.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: avoid silently losing records

Look at `filter(raw, plant_id == "P01")` before using `distinct()`. Do not use
`distinct(plant_id, .keep_all = TRUE)`: it keeps the first row for each ID and
throws away a second row even when the two disagree. Disagreeing records need
investigation.
:::

## Checking your repairs

1. Add a comment above each repair in `day11-cleaning.R` naming the field-note
   entry behind it. Then use
   `filter(cleaned, plant_id %in% c("P06", "P18", "P21"))` to find out whether
   those plants now have the values the notes give. You should see P18 with
   initial length 18.7, P21 with final length 43.8, and P06 with final length `NA`.
2. Use `group_by(treatment)` and `summarise(mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE))` on
   `cleaned` to find out how much each group grew on average. Control gives
   15.21 mm (11 plants) and treated 21.49 mm (12 plants).
3. How much would the P21 slip have mattered? Make a copy in which P21 keeps the
   typed value:
   `slipped <- mutate(cleaned, final_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P21", 4.38, final_mm), growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)`,
   and summarise it the same way. The treated mean drops to 18.21 mm, because P21
   now "grew" −19.2 mm.
4. Make `wrong_zero_example` in the same way, with P06's final length set to 0,
   and use `mean(wrong_zero_example$growth_mm)` to find out what the invented zero
   does to the overall mean. You should get 16.69 mm instead of 18.49 mm.
5. Use `read_csv("data/seedlings-messy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)` with its
   default settings and `str()` to find out what R would have made of this file
   without the text import. The trailing space is silently removed, so only three
   labels remain, and `initial_mm` becomes a text column (`chr`) because of the
   single `18.7 mm` entry, so no mean can be calculated from it.
6. Write `output/cleaning-notes.txt` with one line per problem: the plant, what you
   saw, the evidence, and what you did. End with the plant whose measurement is
   unknown. Then restart R (**Session → Restart R**), rerun the whole script, and
   use `nrow()` to confirm that the raw file still has 25 rows and
   `output/seedlings-cleaned.csv` has 24.

## A second class's data

Another class has sent `data/seedlings-transfer.csv`: 18 seedlings, nine in each
group, measured seven days apart like ours. They sent no field notes. Is the
file ready to use? Start a new script, `day11-transfer.R`.

1. Use `dim()`, `count(plant_id)`, `unique(treatment)` and `sum(is.na())` to find
   out whether the file has one row per plant, two clean labels and complete
   lengths. You should find 18 rows, no repeated ID, only `control` and `treated`,
   and no missing values.
2. Use `mutate()` to calculate `growth_mm` and find out how much T01 grew. Check
   it by hand: 40.3 − 25.3 = 15.0 mm. Save the table with growth as
   `output/day11-transfer-growth.csv`.
3. Write a short handover note, `output/day11-transfer-audit.txt`, saying what you
   checked and what you found. Since nothing was wrong and there are no source
   records, no value was changed. If a value had looked odd, you would keep it and
   ask the recorder.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What makes a repair justified?

A source record, such as the notebook entry for P21. A check only raises the
question; the evidence answers it. A very small or large value may be real and is
kept unless a record shows it was entered wrongly.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The cleaned file has 24 rows but the raw file has 25. Is something lost?

No. The extra row was the identical second P01, removed because the field notes
confirm the duplicate import. All 24 plants are still there; P06 is kept with an
unknown final length.
:::

**Keep:** `day11-cleaning.R`, `output/seedlings-cleaned.csv` and
`output/cleaning-notes.txt`.
